explanation: Fires inside numeric and time expressions: digits that continue a year or count (199[8], 60[0], 201[6]), and duration or rate words after a number or time phrase ('19 years', 'past three decades', 'per fraction', 'year after year'). A few top examples are non-numeric (e.g. 'server-side', 'Guidelines'). Non-numeric prose is weak.

A mixture: the colon or 'family' in taxonomic classifications ('Diptera: Cecidomyiidae', 'a moth in the family X'), the dot in software version numbers (ruby 2.0, LLVM 3.4), code and config punctuation (=, ;, indentation), and pieces of non-Latin script words.

Fires on Go source code syntax, mainly line-initial tab-indented keywords and operators such as 'if', 'for', '!=', '=', '()', and on the word 'Go' as the programming language in prose. There are scattered weaker hits in unrelated prose and non-Latin text.

Two unrelated triggers. (1) A paragraph-initial marker right after a blank line: '...' / '…' or the colon of 'Q:' (strong). (2) 'to' after 'related' and 'entitled' after a document reference ('related to', 'a publication entitled'), which are moderate.

A mixture centered on structured, data-like spans: digits in postal codes and street addresses, unit words after numbers ('13 ounces', '20 seconds', '6 months'), 'address' in 'shipping/mailing address', class or module names in import statements (TypedArray, ZonedDateTime, random), and citation numbers. Ordinary prose is weak.

The letter 'n' (or the following '=') in sample-size notation inside parentheses in scientific text, e.g. '(n = 20)' or 'patients (n = 12)'. It also fires on a few key=value tokens such as 'ou=' or 'CommonName:'. Other uses of n are weak.

The token right before an enumeration index, or the start of an index label: 'Specific Aim [ ]1', 'Part 2', 'Solution 1', footnote markers '[^1]', 'table1', 'script1', zero-padded reference numbers (ref00[1]), 'Group A'. Strength is highest for 'Aim N' in grant abstracts.

No clear shared feature: quantifiers and determiners such as 'most', 'a few', 'many' in several languages (Vietnamese 'những', Indonesian 'banyak', Russian 'несколько', French 'quelques'), mid-word subword pieces of names and technical words, and assorted code tokens. Spam-like or non-English text tends to fire.

Two unrelated jobs. (1) A perfect or past auxiliary or verb right after a subject near the start of a news item or blog post ('X has [been]', 'We've [improved]', 'the ion engine [was]'). (2) Digits or hyphens inside legal docket, case, citation and patent numbers ('NO. WR-17,5[7]5', 'Pat. Nos. 4,46[6],895').

A mixture. The strongest and most consistent hit is 'appeal' in 'This appeal' in court opinions. Others are the '0' in MDPI-style section anchors ('{#sec1-ijerph-17-[0]0783'), package or class name pieces in imports, '<head', and the head noun of headline phrases ('good news', 'Need to Know').

Mostly mid-word subword pieces that continue a multi-token word or name (D'[ALE]SSANDRO, ant[ip]roliferative, Jab[od]etabek, tet[rah]edron, J[ark]). It also fires on function words in Portuguese, French and Spanish text ('a été', 'Se ha') and some code tokens.

Fires on the second or completing token of a set multi-word term or idiom, where the first word predicts it: 'full width', 'short answer', 'Coma Scale', 'foreign key', 'let's face', 'lucky enough', 'Washington University', 'pone' in PLoS citations, 'initWithCGImage'. Free combinations are weak.

The verb or complement right after a modal or negation that expresses (im)possibility or ease: 'cannot [be]', 'can't [be]', 'could not [be]', 'has never [been] easier', 'impossible/difficult [to]', 'may [be] reproduced'. The 't of can't also fires. The same words without a modal or negation context are weak.

Mostly the continuation token of a code namespace, import or URL path (System[.Linq], java.math[.BigInteger], googleapis.com[/ajax], go.microsoft.com[/fwlink], @[inheritdoc], SqlDataAdapter). It also fires on pieces of CJK, Greek and Croatian text and on some word-internal pieces of names.
